item.title: China says acts of Japanese right-wing forces blatantly challenge postwar int'l order
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of National Defense said on Friday that acts by Japanese right-wing forces were clearly challenging the postwar international order, after reports that Japan planned to keep labeling China as its greatest strategic challenge and to consider easing restrictions on nuclear weapons.
Ministry spokesperson Chen Xi said Japan, as a defeated country in World War II, should have reflected on its history of aggression and war crimes, and drawn lessons from history.
"Instead, right-wing forces in Japan keep fabricating false narratives on the so-called China threat, and distorting facts to portray Japan as a victim," Chen said.
He said Japan was ramping up defense expenditure, strengthening offensive and long-range strike capabilities, and, worse still, seeking to progressively ease nuclear restrictions.
"With such moves, they have not only betrayed Japan's commitment to peace, but also blatantly challenged the postwar international order and the authority of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons," he said.
Chen called on the international community to stay highly vigilant and take countermeasures against Japan's push for remilitarization, uphold the international nuclear non-proliferation regime, and defend the security and peace of the world.
The remarks came after reports that Japan would continue to label China as its greatest strategic challenge in its revised three security documents, and increase its defense spending to around 70 to 80 trillion yen (about 438 to 500 billion U.S. dollars) over the next five years.
The Japanese government was also said to be considering amending its National Security Strategy to include exceptions to the three non-nuclear principles, which potentially allows the transport of nuclear weapons into Japan in emergencies.

item.title: China's top diplomat calls for uninterrupted China-US dialogue
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
Wang Yi, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and director of the Office of the Foreign Affairs Commission of the CPC Central Committee, meets with US representatives to the 2026 China-US Party Dialogue in Beijing, China, November 13, 2026. /Foreign Ministry
Top Chinese diplomat Wang Yi on Friday called for sustained dialogue between China and the United States during a meeting with US representatives to the 2026 China-US Political Dialogue in Beijing.
Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and director of the Office of the Foreign Affairs Commission of the CPC Central Committee, said the two countries should maintain continuous exchanges to clarify shared goals, expand mutually beneficial cooperation and consolidate the foundation of bilateral ties, while working to safeguard global peace and stability.
Wang stressed that both sides should uphold the principles of mutual respect, peaceful coexistence and win-win cooperation, and translate into concrete action the common understandings reached by the two heads of state on building a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.
The US representatives said people-to-people exchanges, especially youth and student exchanges, help foster friendship and trust between the two peoples.
They voiced appreciation for the "100,000 Youth in Five Years" initiative, under which 100,000 young Americans will visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years, and pledged to work toward the sound and steady development of US-China relations.

item.title: China willing to further boost political mutual trust with Thailand, says Chinese premier
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
BANGKOK, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Friday that China is willing to work with Thailand to further consolidate the foundation of political mutual trust, support each other's core interests and major concerns, tap cooperation potential in various fields and deliver more tangible results to better benefit the peoples of both countries.
Li made the remarks when meeting with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.
He said Chinese President Xi Jinping met with Anutin during the Thai PM's official visit to China in July, and the two leaders jointly charted the course for the development of China-Thailand relations.
Li said that, with his visit to Thailand, the prime ministers of the two countries have exchanged visits within four months, fully demonstrating the high level of bilateral relations.
Noting that both China and Thailand are at an important stage of national development, Li said China firmly supports the Thai government in smoothly carrying out its work.
China is willing to work with Thailand to make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers and the joint committee on economic and trade cooperation, Li said.
China stands ready to work with Thailand to strengthen the alignment of development strategies, advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and key projects such as the China-Thailand railway, and accelerate consultations on a new five-year plan for economic and trade cooperation, Li said.
He added that China is ready to promote the early realization of mutual protection of geographical indication products, and expand cooperation in such fields as finance, new energy, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence, so as to achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes at a higher level.
China is ready to import more quality products from Thailand and encourages Chinese companies to invest and do business in the Southeast Asian country, he said, adding that China hopes the Thai side will provide a fair, stable and predictable business environment for Chinese companies.
The two sides, Li said, should also strengthen exchanges and cooperation in areas including disaster prevention and mitigation, water resources management, education, tourism and media, and step up efforts to combat illegal and criminal activities, to enhance the people's sense of gain from China-Thailand cooperation.
At present, the international situation remains fraught with instability and uncertainty, Li said, noting that China is willing to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Thailand under multilateral frameworks including China-ASEAN, the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation, the United Nations, the World Trade Organization and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, so as to contribute to global peace and development.
For his part, Anutin said Thailand attaches great importance to its relations with China and is committed to advancing all-round cooperation between the two countries and continuously elevating the Thailand-China comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership to new heights, bringing greater benefits to the two peoples.
Thailand is willing to strengthen high-level exchanges with China, make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers of the two countries, expand bilateral trade, and deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in fields including agriculture, finance, connectivity, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, e-commerce, and science and technology, said the Thai prime minister.
Thailand is ready to continue providing a favorable business environment for Chinese enterprises investing in Thailand, strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation with China to combat online gambling, telecom and online fraud among other crimes, ensure the safety of Chinese tourists, and deepen people-to-people and cultural exchanges to consolidate the foundation of public friendship, Anutin said.
Thailand supports China's successful hosting of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and stands ready to work with China to ensure the success of the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation Leaders' Meeting, making new contributions to regional stability, development and prosperity, said the Thai prime minister.
Following the talks, the two leaders witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering the fields including the automotive industry, vocational education, agriculture, customs and security.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Yin Bogu)

item.title: Xi stresses persevering with full, rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to provide strong guarantees for SOEs and state capital to get stronger, do better, and grow bigger.
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction on Party building in SOEs.
He noted that Party building in SOEs has been strengthened and new progress has been made across the board since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012.
Xi urged further efforts to uphold and strengthen the Party's overall leadership of SOEs, better integrate the Party's leadership into all links of corporate governance, advance in-depth integration of Party building with production and operation, foster high-caliber, professional teams, and build good conduct, enforce discipline and fight corruption.
Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and a member of the CPC Central Committee Secretariat, speaks at a meeting on Party building in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 13, 2026. An important instruction by Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed at the meeting held in Beijing on Friday. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei)
The instruction was conveyed at a meeting on Party building in SOEs held in Beijing on Friday. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and a member of the Secretariat of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event.
Cai said Xi's important instruction has charted the course for further strengthening Party building in SOEs. Cai emphasized the need to accurately grasp the new requirements for Party building in SOEs arising from the evolving global, national and Party conditions. He called for efforts to resolutely combat corruption and further institutionalize and standardize the Party's leadership over SOEs.

item.title: I will never forget you -- An American elder's cross-Pacific nostalgia for China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
* At 18, David bid farewell to Huangyuan with his family on a drizzly day. Thinking it was merely a short trip, they left their furniture and bedding sealed in the old house as they were -- no one imagined the farewell would stretch to 38 years.
* David spent his childhood and adolescence in Huangyuan. More than three decades later, he returned to his "hometown" over 20 times, doing everything in his power to help the local people and leaving behind one touching story after another.
* "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family."
by Xinhua writers Wang Jinjin, Xie Tongqiang, Jiang Yi
XINING, China, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- "Have you had dinner yet?" White-haired David Plymire spoke in fluent Huangyuan dialect, leaning toward the webcam in his living room in Springfield, Missouri.
His greetings traveled across the Pacific, reaching Tongkhor Ancient Town in Huangyuan County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. "Yes, we have! We're waiting to see you on video!" David's longtime friend Wang Shikang replied from in front of the screen, eager to catch a glimpse of their old friend on the other end of the video call.
CENTURY-OLD FRIENDSHIP
In the 1920s, David's father, Victor Plymire, arrived in Tongkhor town along the ancient Tea Horse Road. In 1932, one-year-old David was brought to the small plateau town, where he spent the next 17 years growing up and came to regard it as his hometown.
Time has taken its toll. The trans-Pacific journey has become too physically demanding for David over the past decade.
"We all miss you! Almost ten years have passed since you were last able to come to Huangyuan. People here, young and old, miss you," Wang said, waving at him through the screen.
Wang told David that they were making the video call from the ancient town's old streets, where many historic buildings had been restored with the help of photographs taken decades earlier by his father, Victor.
This file family photo shows David V. Plymire (2nd L), his father Victor G. Plymire (1st L), his mother (R, back) and his sister Mary Ann Plymire. (Xinhua)
A century ago, Victor took his camera around Tongkhor, documenting its streets, scenery and residents and leaving behind a unique visual record of life on the plateau. The photographs were later compiled into an album titled Imprint of a Legacy.
Dong Baoming, general manager of Huangyuan Dancheng Tourism Development Co., Ltd., said Victor and David's photographs had helped bring the town's past back to life. The images now fill the Imprints exhibition hall, which has opened to the public, offering visitors a glimpse of Huangyuan as it once was.
One moment during the call was particularly poignant. Bai Qiming, son of Bai Yongsheng, David's childhood friend known locally as "Ga Liang-ge," sent his greetings to David through the screen and spoke of how they had missed each other over the years. David fell silent for several seconds before quietly saying, "I can't come back now."
TRANS-PACIFIC MEMORIES
"Has the weather turned cold there?" David asked, then went on reminiscing about swimming in the town's river in summer and skating on the ice in winter when he was a boy.
Memories came flooding back as David recalled how arduous travel had once been. A journey from Huangyuan to Xining took an entire day, with a stop at Zhamalong along the way for a bowl of noodles.
"Do you have suanjiujiu (sea buckthorn)? Could you send me some suanjiujiu juice?" David asked with a childlike smile.
Wang Shikang (R), the former head of the Huangyuan County People's Hospital, Huang Jiong (C), the current head of the hospital, and Bai Qiming, son of David V. Plymire's childhood friend Bai Yongsheng, greet David V. Plymire during a video meeting on Nov. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Long)
Wang jokingly reminded David that he had sent him 3 kg of tsampa 15 years ago. David said he had carefully kept the package in his refrigerator ever since. He then recalled hand-grabbed mutton, pickled cabbage and Laba porridge. His longing for the familiar flavors of home and the warmth of everyday life back in Huangyuan went far beyond what the screen could convey.
During the video call, David watched a prerecorded video of greetings from Huangyuan residents. Leaning back in his chair, he listened and watched attentively, looking closely at the familiar faces on the screen, sometimes breaking into hearty laughter.
"My body is here, but my heart is in Huangyuan. I wish everyone back home peace and happiness," David said.
As the conversation turned to shehuo, traditional festive performances held around the Chinese New Year, David spontaneously recited a children's rhyme from Huangyuan that he had known since boyhood: "On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, the temple gates swing open; village women come to light incense."
ENDURING DEVOTION TO HOMETOWN
David's correspondence with Wang, then director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, is preserved in the hospital's history exhibition hall. Several letters reveal a recurring subject: a CT scanner.
In their early letters, the two addressed each other formally as "Director Wang" and "Mr. Plymire," discussing practical matters such as customs clearance. But with each of David's return visits to his hometown, the formality gradually melted away, giving rise to the warmer, more familiar terms "old friend" and "brother."
Between 1997 and 1999, David made three trips to bring the CT scanner to Huangyuan. When the hospital could not afford the 500,000 yuan (75,000 U.S. dollars) tax bill, he rallied support to cover every penny.
The scanner enabled the hospital's first brain surgery and helped save countless lives over its 15 years of service. Today, it rests in the hospital's history exhibition hall, alongside archival records documenting his many other contributions.
This file photo taken in March 1989 shows David V. Plymire (C) posing for photos with hospital staff after donating medical equipment to the Huangyuan County People's Hospital, in Huangyuan County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. (Xinhua)
"Mr. Plymire did more than simply donate a few pieces of equipment. He brought us a powerful source of inspiration," said Huang Jiong, director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, visibly moved. He noted that David has tirelessly raised funds and mobilized support over the past three decades, helping secure donations of more than 30 pieces of medical equipment, worth a total of 6 million yuan (900,000 dollars).
"My hometown has become part of who I am. My flesh and bones are the flesh and bones of Huangyuan," David said during the video call.
Speaking about people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States, David slowly switched to English: "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family."
"Although I can no longer come back to visit because I am too old to travel by plane, I remember everyone. In my memories, I still walk along those streets, travel through the countryside, stand beside the rivers and talk with my friends," he said.
"I shall always remember you in this life, and I will never forget you in the next."

item.title: Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, related events in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping will chair the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting and deliver remarks, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced Friday.
The meeting will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the spokesperson said.
The APEC CEO Summit will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 17 to 18 under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the spokesperson said, adding that President Xi will attend the opening ceremony and deliver a keynote speech.
President Xi will hold a welcome banquet for participating leaders and representatives, and hold bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the meeting, the spokesperson added.

item.title: China holds gathering to mark 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12
A gathering to commemorate the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth is held in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao)
BEIJING, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday held a gathering in Beijing to commemorate the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, addressed the gathering.
Also present at the event were Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee.
More than a century ago, Sun led the Revolution of 1911 to abolish the absolute monarchy that had ruled China for thousands of years. He died in 1925.

item.title: This robot ran a half-marathon in just 50 minutes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
At a half-marathon event in Beijing, China, humanoid robots raced alongside thousands of human runners in separate lanes. One autonomous robot, Lightning, finished in just 50 minutes and 26 seconds—faster than the men’s half-marathon world-record time at the time. A remarkable test of speed, balance and endurance.

item.title: Can China's robots pick tomatoes without bruising them?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Picking cherry tomatoes is trickier than it looks. At a 2026 agricultural robotics competition in China, machines equipped with cameras and robotic arms take on a delicate challenge: harvesting small tomatoes without damaging them. Can they match the precision of human hands?

item.title: How China is rebuilding 3,000-year-old bronze treasures
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
How do you put ancient treasures back together after thousands of years? At China's Sanxingdui archaeological site, conservators combine meticulous hands-on restoration with 3D scanning and digital modeling to study broken bronze artifacts and help reveal the extraordinary craftsmanship of ancient Shu civilization.
